top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: A 2022 systematic review examined the impact of opioids on adults during and after their ED stay. 49 They concluded that, 'Opioids may have pain outcomes equivalent to those of NSAIDs, but evidence on comparisons of harms is very uncertain and heterogeneous.' However, they did not perform a meta-­ analysis. Nevertheless, they only included two studies on opioids prescribed upon ED discharge, which were included in our study. 37,42 We identified two other adult studies 38,39 with data on opioids after discharge from the ED that they included only in the 'opioids prescribed in the ED' section. A systematic review published in 2020 evaluated outpatient acute pain management (medication and other approaches) from non-­ low-­ back musculoskeletal injuries in adults and found that opioids combined with acetaminophen compared to placebo improved pain from Day 1 to 7, but not for immediate pain (less than 2 h), and caused more adverse events. 22 However, they included all parallel-­ design studies on musculoskeletal injuries in any outpatient setting and studies with a single dose of opioids; results could be different for acute pain management in an ED-­ discharged population. The efficacy of treatment (medication and other approaches) for acute and subacute nonspecific low-­ back pain has been examined in another systematic review. 50 They concluded that to reduce pain intensity, the most efficacious interventions (up to 1 week) were heat wrap, manual therapy, exercise, NSAIDs, and opioids; mild or moderate adverse events were most often associated with opioids, NSAIDs, and steroids. However, they identified only three studies on opioids; two were performed in the ED and one was conducted in an outpatient setting using meptazinol, 51 which is seldomly used and available only in a few European countries.

top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Five studies 38-­ 42 were at low risk of bias and only one study 37 on adults with an ankle sprain was at high risk of bias because of the lack of intervention allocation concealment and different baseline characteristics. Nevertheless, after removing this study in a sensitivity analysis, results were similar which demonstrates their consistency. There was significant heterogeneity in results from studies on opioid efficacy, but this was mostly due to the poor analgesic effect of codeine. Heterogeneity was very low for studies using opioids other than codeine, as it was for adverse events associated with opioids in general. Furthermore, one study 42 on acute low-­ back pain found that adding oxycodone/acetaminophen to naproxen alone did not improve functional outcomes or pain at 1-­ week follow-­ up. In this study the oxycodone/acetaminophen was prescribed every 8 h as needed; since the elimination half-­ life of oxycodone is 3.51 h (SD ± 1.43) 47 and that oxycodone is typically given every 4 to 6 h, 48 this could explain the ineffectiveness of oxycodone. Systematic reviews on specific painful conditions obtained results aligned with ours. For osteoarthritis pain, one review concluded with overall low confidence that the effect of NSAIDs for knee pain was similar to that of opioids. 52 However, another systematic review on osteoarthritis not limited to the knee found that opioids may provide a small benefit in pain and disability but may also increase the risk of adverse events. As they did not encounter a study using codeine, their results are comparable to our sensitivity analysis excluding codeine. 53 Moreover, a systematic review on postoperative pain demonstrated that codeine provides less pain relief and more adverse events than NSAIDs. 19 Another study, evaluating codeine/acetaminophen and oxycodone/acetaminophen combinations on the first day after ED discharge, demonstrated a not statistically significant trend in more pain relief with oxycodone/acetaminophen (66% vs. 61%). 54 However, one review examined the outpatient treatment of acute pain in general (surgical and nonsurgical) and concluded that opioid therapy was associated with similar efficacy as an NSAID and increased risk of short-­ term adverse events. 18

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: In collaboration with an information specialist, we developed a search strategy based on four search themes: 'opioid,' 'pain,' 'emergency,' and 'effectiveness' (detailed search strategies are available in Supplement Methods S1 ). The following databases were searched from their inception to May 5, 2022: CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. An updated search was performed at the end of the process during the third week of January 2023 to collect recently published papers. We also searched Clini calTr ials.gov and the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number registry for ongoing studies. Gray literature was searched using Google Scholar and the first 300 hits were screened to identify any relevant studies. References from studies meeting inclusion criteria were examined and their authors were contacted to identify additional relevant studies.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.

top_evidence.text: Raoul Daoust, MD, MSc, Emergency Department, Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal, 5400 Gouin Blvd. West, Montreal, Québec H4J 1C5, Canada. Email: raoul.daoust@umontreal.ca Background: Opioids are often prescribed for acute pain to patients discharged from the emergency department (ED), but there is a paucity of data on their short-­ term use. The purpose of this study was to synthesize the evidence regarding the efficacy of prescribed opioids compared to nonopioid analgesics for acute pain relief in ED-­ discharged patients.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: This meta-­ analysis of studies originating from the United States and Canada on adult and pediatric populations showed that opioids are not more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs) in managing acute pain after ED discharge. However, a sensitivity analysis showed that opioids other than codeine provided better pain relief than nonopioids. Additionally, opioids were associated in all studies with a higher rate of adverse events and in one study with higher use of rescue medications. 41 While we planned to include RCTs on all types of acute outpatient pain management after ED discharge, we found only studies including patients with musculoskeletal injuries. top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.

top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The difference in pain intensity scores (or in pain relief) between patients who were administered opioids versus those not administered opioids from baseline to cutoff time as specified in the original RCT (the final single time point from each follow-­ up were used for the main analysis), adverse events incidence, utilization of rescue analgesics, and data related to patient demographics were reported for each study. If data were available for at least three studies, results for the main outcome and for adverse events were pooled and meta-­ analyzed. For the main efficacy outcome, studies that reported mean and standard deviation (SD) of pain relief for both opioid and nonopioid groups were expressed by standard mean differences (SMD) in forest plots. For studies that presented the percentage of patients with pain relief or with treatment failure, data were converted to SMD using a meta-­ analysis software (Comprehensive Meta-­ analysis: A Computer Program for Research Synthesis, Biostat, 2005). 32 Data extracted for adverse events were all reported with the percentage of patients with | any side effects and were expressed in odds ratios (ORs). Sensitivity analyses were performed for studies with available short-­ term follow-­ up (≤3 days) to examine whether opioids were more effective in this situation. Another sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids since codeine is a prodrug and its analgesic properties depend on its conversion to morphine, which varies considerably between subjects. 33 Sensitivity analyses were also performed excluding studies with high risk of bias and for studies involving a pediatric population compared to adults. Finally, we repeated the same analyses while excluding studies for which the comparator was only a placebo. Heterogeneity was statistically assessed both overall and for each sensitivity analysis using I 2 , tau-­ square, and Cochran's Q tests. Prediction intervals were not presented since they can be problematic when the number of studies is small ( n < 10). 34 A chi-­ square test was used to determine whether there was a difference between sensitivity categories. All effect sizes are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All analyses were conducted using an inverse variance weighting method and a random-­ effect model, even if the I 2 was low, due to the clinical heterogeneity of painful conditions, outcomes, and treatments. 35 Forest plots were performed using Revman, version 5.4 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2014). No tests for publication bias were done (funnel plot asymmetry) because the power of the test is too low to distinguish chance from real asymmetry when there are fewer than 10 studies. 34

top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

The following databases were searched from their inception to May 5, 2022: CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. top_evidence.text: Risk of bias was assessed using the Effective Practice and Organization of Care (EPOC) risk-­ of-­ bias tool. 31 Two reviewers (JP and MM) assessed the risk of bias independently, with conflicts resolved through discussion or involvement of a third reviewer (RD). RCTs were ranked as having low risk, being unclear, or having high risk of bias across nine domains (i.e., random sequence generation, allocation concealment, similarity of baseline outcome measurements, similarity of baseline characteristics, incomplete outcome data, knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately prevented during the study, protection against contamination, selective outcome reporting, and other risk of bias) and the overall risk of bias was derived. Risk-­ of-­ bias judgments for each domain across studies were summarized using risk-­ of-­ bias graphs and summaries. Unpublished studies were considered at high risk of bias.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: We included randomized controlled trials (RCT) and cluster RCTs designed to evaluate the efficacy of opioids prescribed for relief of acute pain in ED-­ discharged patients compared to nonopioid analgesics. All types of pain complaints were considered. We excluded studies exclusively on patients with substance use disorder or chronic pain, evaluating only opioids given during the ED stay, comparing different opioids head-­ to-­ head, not reporting pain intensities or pain relief (after contacting authors), or available only as abstracts. There were no exclusions based on language or date of publication.

top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The difference in pain intensity scores (or in pain relief) between patients who were administered opioids versus those not administered opioids from baseline to cutoff time as specified in the original RCT (the final single time point from each follow-­ up were used for the main analysis), adverse events incidence, utilization of rescue analgesics, and data related to patient demographics were reported for each study. If data were available for at least three studies, results for the main outcome and for adverse events were pooled and meta-­ analyzed. For the main efficacy outcome, studies that reported mean and standard deviation (SD) of pain relief for both opioid and nonopioid groups were expressed by standard mean differences (SMD) in forest plots. For studies that presented the percentage of patients with pain relief or with treatment failure, data were converted to SMD using a meta-­ analysis software (Comprehensive Meta-­ analysis: A Computer Program for Research Synthesis, Biostat, 2005). 32 Data extracted for adverse events were all reported with the percentage of patients with | any side effects and were expressed in odds ratios (ORs). Sensitivity analyses were performed for studies with available short-­ term follow-­ up (≤3 days) to examine whether opioids were more effective in this situation. Another sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids since codeine is a prodrug and its analgesic properties depend on its conversion to morphine, which varies considerably between subjects. 33 Sensitivity analyses were also performed excluding studies with high risk of bias and for studies involving a pediatric population compared to adults. Finally, we repeated the same analyses while excluding studies for which the comparator was only a placebo. Heterogeneity was statistically assessed both overall and for each sensitivity analysis using I 2 , tau-­ square, and Cochran's Q tests. Prediction intervals were not presented since they can be problematic when the number of studies is small ( n < 10). 34 A chi-­ square test was used to determine whether there was a difference between sensitivity categories. All effect sizes are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All analyses were conducted using an inverse variance weighting method and a random-­ effect model, even if the I 2 was low, due to the clinical heterogeneity of painful conditions, outcomes, and treatments. 35 Forest plots were performed using Revman, version 5.4 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2014). No tests for publication bias were done (funnel plot asymmetry) because the power of the test is too low to distinguish chance from real asymmetry when there are fewer than 10 studies. 34

The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

top_evidence.text: Five studies 38-­ 42 were at low risk of bias and only one study 37 on adults with an ankle sprain was at high risk of bias because of the lack of intervention allocation concealment and different baseline characteristics. Nevertheless, after removing this study in a sensitivity analysis, results were similar which demonstrates their consistency. There was significant heterogeneity in results from studies on opioid efficacy, but this was mostly due to the poor analgesic effect of codeine. Heterogeneity was very low for studies using opioids other than codeine, as it was for adverse events associated with opioids in general. Furthermore, one study 42 on acute low-­ back pain found that adding oxycodone/acetaminophen to naproxen alone did not improve functional outcomes or pain at 1-­ week follow-­ up. In this study the oxycodone/acetaminophen was prescribed every 8 h as needed; since the elimination half-­ life of oxycodone is 3.51 h (SD ± 1.43) 47 and that oxycodone is typically given every 4 to 6 h, 48 this could explain the ineffectiveness of oxycodone. Systematic reviews on specific painful conditions obtained results aligned with ours. For osteoarthritis pain, one review concluded with overall low confidence that the effect of NSAIDs for knee pain was similar to that of opioids. 52 However, another systematic review on osteoarthritis not limited to the knee found that opioids may provide a small benefit in pain and disability but may also increase the risk of adverse events. As they did not encounter a study using codeine, their results are comparable to our sensitivity analysis excluding codeine. 53 Moreover, a systematic review on postoperative pain demonstrated that codeine provides less pain relief and more adverse events than NSAIDs. 19 Another study, evaluating codeine/acetaminophen and oxycodone/acetaminophen combinations on the first day after ED discharge, demonstrated a not statistically significant trend in more pain relief with oxycodone/acetaminophen (66% vs. 61%). 54 However, one review examined the outpatient treatment of acute pain in general (surgical and nonsurgical) and concluded that opioid therapy was associated with similar efficacy as an NSAID and increased risk of short-­ term adverse events. 18

top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The difference in pain intensity scores (or in pain relief) between patients who were administered opioids versus those not administered opioids from baseline to cutoff time as specified in the original RCT (the final single time point from each follow-­ up were used for the main analysis), adverse events incidence, utilization of rescue analgesics, and data related to patient demographics were reported for each study. If data were available for at least three studies, results for the main outcome and for adverse events were pooled and meta-­ analyzed. For the main efficacy outcome, studies that reported mean and standard deviation (SD) of pain relief for both opioid and nonopioid groups were expressed by standard mean differences (SMD) in forest plots. For studies that presented the percentage of patients with pain relief or with treatment failure, data were converted to SMD using a meta-­ analysis software (Comprehensive Meta-­ analysis: A Computer Program for Research Synthesis, Biostat, 2005). 32 Data extracted for adverse events were all reported with the percentage of patients with | any side effects and were expressed in odds ratios (ORs). Sensitivity analyses were performed for studies with available short-­ term follow-­ up (≤3 days) to examine whether opioids were more effective in this situation. Another sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids since codeine is a prodrug and its analgesic properties depend on its conversion to morphine, which varies considerably between subjects. 33 Sensitivity analyses were also performed excluding studies with high risk of bias and for studies involving a pediatric population compared to adults. Finally, we repeated the same analyses while excluding studies for which the comparator was only a placebo. Heterogeneity was statistically assessed both overall and for each sensitivity analysis using I 2 , tau-­ square, and Cochran's Q tests. Prediction intervals were not presented since they can be problematic when the number of studies is small ( n < 10). 34 A chi-­ square test was used to determine whether there was a difference between sensitivity categories. All effect sizes are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All analyses were conducted using an inverse variance weighting method and a random-­ effect model, even if the I 2 was low, due to the clinical heterogeneity of painful conditions, outcomes, and treatments. 35 Forest plots were performed using Revman, version 5.4 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2014). No tests for publication bias were done (funnel plot asymmetry) because the power of the test is too low to distinguish chance from real asymmetry when there are fewer than 10 studies. 34

All types of pain complaints were considered. We excluded studies exclusively on patients with substance use disorder or chronic pain, evaluating only opioids given during the ED stay, comparing different opioids head-­ to-­ head, not reporting pain intensities or pain relief (after contacting authors), or available only as abstracts. There were no exclusions based on language or date of publication.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The difference in pain intensity scores (or in pain relief) between patients who were administered opioids versus those not administered opioids from baseline to cutoff time as specified in the original RCT (the final single time point from each follow-­ up were used for the main analysis), adverse events incidence, utilization of rescue analgesics, and data related to patient demographics were reported for each study. If data were available for at least three studies, results for the main outcome and for adverse events were pooled and meta-­ analyzed. For the main efficacy outcome, studies that reported mean and standard deviation (SD) of pain relief for both opioid and nonopioid groups were expressed by standard mean differences (SMD) in forest plots. For studies that presented the percentage of patients with pain relief or with treatment failure, data were converted to SMD using a meta-­ analysis software (Comprehensive Meta-­ analysis: A Computer Program for Research Synthesis, Biostat, 2005). 32 Data extracted for adverse events were all reported with the percentage of patients with | any side effects and were expressed in odds ratios (ORs). Sensitivity analyses were performed for studies with available short-­ term follow-­ up (≤3 days) to examine whether opioids were more effective in this situation. Another sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids since codeine is a prodrug and its analgesic properties depend on its conversion to morphine, which varies considerably between subjects. 33 Sensitivity analyses were also performed excluding studies with high risk of bias and for studies involving a pediatric population compared to adults. Finally, we repeated the same analyses while excluding studies for which the comparator was only a placebo. Heterogeneity was statistically assessed both overall and for each sensitivity analysis using I 2 , tau-­ square, and Cochran's Q tests. Prediction intervals were not presented since they can be problematic when the number of studies is small ( n < 10). 34 A chi-­ square test was used to determine whether there was a difference between sensitivity categories. All effect sizes are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All analyses were conducted using an inverse variance weighting method and a random-­ effect model, even if the I 2 was low, due to the clinical heterogeneity of painful conditions, outcomes, and treatments. 35 Forest plots were performed using Revman, version 5.4 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2014). No tests for publication bias were done (funnel plot asymmetry) because the power of the test is too low to distinguish chance from real asymmetry when there are fewer than 10 studies. 34

top_evidence.text: Risk of bias was assessed using the Effective Practice and Organization of Care (EPOC) risk-­ of-­ bias tool. 31 Two reviewers (JP and MM) assessed the risk of bias independently, with conflicts resolved through discussion or involvement of a third reviewer (RD). RCTs were ranked as having low risk, being unclear, or having high risk of bias across nine domains (i.e., random sequence generation, allocation concealment, similarity of baseline outcome measurements, similarity of baseline characteristics, incomplete outcome data, knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately prevented during the study, protection against contamination, selective outcome reporting, and other risk of bias) and the overall risk of bias was derived. Risk-­ of-­ bias judgments for each domain across studies were summarized using risk-­ of-­ bias graphs and summaries. Unpublished studies were considered at high risk of bias.

top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

top_evidence.text: In collaboration with an information specialist, we developed a search strategy based on four search themes: 'opioid,' 'pain,' 'emergency,' and 'effectiveness' (detailed search strategies are available in Supplement Methods S1 ). The following databases were searched from their inception to May 5, 2022: CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. An updated search was performed at the end of the process during the third week of January 2023 to collect recently published papers. We also searched Clini calTr ials.gov and the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number registry for ongoing studies. Gray literature was searched using Google Scholar and the first 300 hits were screened to identify any relevant studies. References from studies meeting inclusion criteria were examined and their authors were contacted to identify additional relevant studies.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The difference in pain intensity scores (or in pain relief) between patients who were administered opioids versus those not administered opioids from baseline to cutoff time as specified in the original RCT (the final single time point from each follow-­ up were used for the main analysis), adverse events incidence, utilization of rescue analgesics, and data related to patient demographics were reported for each study. If data were available for at least three studies, results for the main outcome and for adverse events were pooled and meta-­ analyzed. For the main efficacy outcome, studies that reported mean and standard deviation (SD) of pain relief for both opioid and nonopioid groups were expressed by standard mean differences (SMD) in forest plots. For studies that presented the percentage of patients with pain relief or with treatment failure, data were converted to SMD using a meta-­ analysis software (Comprehensive Meta-­ analysis: A Computer Program for Research Synthesis, Biostat, 2005). 32 Data extracted for adverse events were all reported with the percentage of patients with | any side effects and were expressed in odds ratios (ORs). Sensitivity analyses were performed for studies with available short-­ term follow-­ up (≤3 days) to examine whether opioids were more effective in this situation. Another sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids since codeine is a prodrug and its analgesic properties depend on its conversion to morphine, which varies considerably between subjects. 33 Sensitivity analyses were also performed excluding studies with high risk of bias and for studies involving a pediatric population compared to adults. Finally, we repeated the same analyses while excluding studies for which the comparator was only a placebo. Heterogeneity was statistically assessed both overall and for each sensitivity analysis using I 2 , tau-­ square, and Cochran's Q tests. Prediction intervals were not presented since they can be problematic when the number of studies is small ( n < 10). 34 A chi-­ square test was used to determine whether there was a difference between sensitivity categories. All effect sizes are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All analyses were conducted using an inverse variance weighting method and a random-­ effect model, even if the I 2 was low, due to the clinical heterogeneity of painful conditions, outcomes, and treatments. 35 Forest plots were performed using Revman, version 5.4 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2014). No tests for publication bias were done (funnel plot asymmetry) because the power of the test is too low to distinguish chance from real asymmetry when there are fewer than 10 studies. 34

Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.text: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

RCTs were ranked as having low risk, being unclear, or having high risk of bias across nine domains (i.e., random sequence generation, allocation concealment, similarity of baseline outcome measurements, similarity of baseline characteristics, incomplete outcome data, knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately prevented during the study, protection against contamination, selective outcome reporting, and other risk of bias) and the overall risk of bias was derived. top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Five studies 38-­ 42 were at low risk of bias and only one study 37 on adults with an ankle sprain was at high risk of bias because of the lack of intervention allocation concealment and different baseline characteristics. Nevertheless, after removing this study in a sensitivity analysis, results were similar which demonstrates their consistency. There was significant heterogeneity in results from studies on opioid efficacy, but this was mostly due to the poor analgesic effect of codeine. Heterogeneity was very low for studies using opioids other than codeine, as it was for adverse events associated with opioids in general. Furthermore, one study 42 on acute low-­ back pain found that adding oxycodone/acetaminophen to naproxen alone did not improve functional outcomes or pain at 1-­ week follow-­ up. In this study the oxycodone/acetaminophen was prescribed every 8 h as needed; since the elimination half-­ life of oxycodone is 3.51 h (SD ± 1.43) 47 and that oxycodone is typically given every 4 to 6 h, 48 this could explain the ineffectiveness of oxycodone. Systematic reviews on specific painful conditions obtained results aligned with ours. For osteoarthritis pain, one review concluded with overall low confidence that the effect of NSAIDs for knee pain was similar to that of opioids. 52 However, another systematic review on osteoarthritis not limited to the knee found that opioids may provide a small benefit in pain and disability but may also increase the risk of adverse events. As they did not encounter a study using codeine, their results are comparable to our sensitivity analysis excluding codeine. 53 Moreover, a systematic review on postoperative pain demonstrated that codeine provides less pain relief and more adverse events than NSAIDs. 19 Another study, evaluating codeine/acetaminophen and oxycodone/acetaminophen combinations on the first day after ED discharge, demonstrated a not statistically significant trend in more pain relief with oxycodone/acetaminophen (66% vs. 61%). 54 However, one review examined the outpatient treatment of acute pain in general (surgical and nonsurgical) and concluded that opioid therapy was associated with similar efficacy as an NSAID and increased risk of short-­ term adverse events. 18

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.
