top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: In summary, this meta-­ analysis demonstrated that for ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as other opioids are more effective than nonopioids (mostly nonsteroidal anti-­ inflammatory drugs) but also associated with more adverse events. Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

RCTs were ranked as having low risk, being unclear, or having high risk of bias across nine domains (i.e., random sequence generation, allocation concealment, similarity of baseline outcome measurements, similarity of baseline characteristics, incomplete outcome data, knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately prevented during the study, protection against contamination, selective outcome reporting, and other risk of bias) and the overall risk of bias was derived. top_evidence.text: In collaboration with an information specialist, we developed a search strategy based on four search themes: 'opioid,' 'pain,' 'emergency,' and 'effectiveness' (detailed search strategies are available in Supplement Methods S1 ). The following databases were searched from their inception to May 5, 2022: CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. An updated search was performed at the end of the process during the third week of January 2023 to collect recently published papers. We also searched Clini calTr ials.gov and the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number registry for ongoing studies. Gray literature was searched using Google Scholar and the first 300 hits were screened to identify any relevant studies. References from studies meeting inclusion criteria were examined and their authors were contacted to identify additional relevant studies.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The results of opioid efficacy for studies with data on a short-­ term follow-­ up (≤3 days) 38-­ 41 or without the study at high risk of bias 37 were similar as those reported from the main analysis (SMD 0.12, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.45, I 2 = 77%; and SMD 0.12, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.37, I 2 = 69%; Supplement Figures S2 and S3 ). Adult patients treated with opioids had better pain relief than those treated with nonopioids (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42, I 2 = 0%; Supplement Figure S4 ) contrary to children who had nonsignificant difference between opioids and nonopioids ( p = 0.78). However, the comparison of studies with pediatric versus adult patients showed no statistically significant difference between these subgroups ( χ 2 = 1.78, p = 0.18). When we removed the study 39 that had a placebo as a comparator in the adult subgroup, the effect was similar but was no longer statistically significant (SMD 0.16, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.38, I 2 = 0%; Supplement Figure S5 ). The comparison of studies using codeine versus opioids other than codeine showed a significant difference between these subgroups ( χ 2 = 7.47, p = 0.006). Codeine was not more effective than nonopioid medications (SMD -0.12, 95% CI -0.38 to 0.14, | I 2 = 19%). However, patients treated with other opioids than codeine had better pain relief than those treated with nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45, I 2 = 0%; Figure 4 ). Results without the only study at high risk of bias 37 were identical for opioids other than codeine since that study was done with codeine (Supplement Figure S6 ). Also, when removing the study 39 that had a placebo as a comparator in the opioids other than codeine subgroup, the direction of the effect remained but was no longer statistically significant ( p = 0.06, SMD 0.22, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.44, I 2 = 0%; Supplement Figure S7 ).

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.

top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.text: This meta-­ analysis of studies originating from the United States and Canada on adult and pediatric populations showed that opioids are not more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs) in managing acute pain after ED discharge. However, a sensitivity analysis showed that opioids other than codeine provided better pain relief than nonopioids. Additionally, opioids were associated in all studies with a higher rate of adverse events and in one study with higher use of rescue medications. 41 While we planned to include RCTs on all types of acute outpatient pain management after ED discharge, we found only studies including patients with musculoskeletal injuries. We did not observe a significant difference in results between adult and pediatric populations. FIGURE 2 Forest plot of opioid efficacy after ED discharge. top_evidence.text: In summary, this meta-­ analysis demonstrated that for ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as other opioids are more effective than nonopioids (mostly nonsteroidal anti-­ inflammatory drugs) but also associated with more adverse events. Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

There were no exclusions based on language or date of publication.

An updated search was performed at the end of the process during the third week of January 2023 to collect recently published papers. We also searched Clini calTr ials.gov and the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number registry for ongoing studies. Gray literature was searched using Google Scholar and the first 300 hits were screened to identify any relevant studies. References from studies meeting inclusion criteria were examined and their authors were contacted to identify additional relevant studies.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: This systematic review and meta-­ analysis was prospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD42022332009). Its results are presented as per the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-­ Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines (Data S1). 29 We also followed et al . the synthesis without meta-­ analysis reporting guidelines to complement the PRISMA guidelines. 30

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Identified references from all databases were transferred to Covidence systematic review manager (Covidence systematic review software, Veritas Health Innovation, available at www.covid ence.org). Eight reviewers (RD, JP, MM, DW, GF, AF, AO, and AC) participated in a two-­ stage selection process of eligible studies. After duplicate removal, each citation was screened by two independent reviewers using the title and abstract for potential relevance. The full text of the remaining citations was then independently evaluated by two reviewers against inclusion and exclusion criteria. During both stages, a third reviewer (RD or AC) resolved discrepancies.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: This project received funding from the Fonds des Urgentistes de l'Hôpital du Sacré-­ Coeur de Montréal. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and gray literature databases were searched from inception to January 2023. Two independent reviewers selected randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of prescribed opioids for ED-­ discharged patients, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Authors were contacted for missing data and to identify additional studies. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief. All meta-­ analyses used a random-­ effect model and a sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids. Trial registration Registered with Prospero #CRD42022332009. Supervising Editor: James Miner This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2023 The Authors. Academic Emergency Medicine published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. | ﻿   | Results: From 5419 initially screened citations, 46 full texts were evaluated and six studies enrolling 1161 patients were included. Risk of bias was low for five studies. There was no statistically significant difference in pain intensity scores or pain relief between opioids versus nonopioid analgesics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.10 to 0.34). Contrary to children, adult patients treated with opioid had better pain relief (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.13-­ 0.42) compared to nonopioids. In another sensitivity analysis excluding studies using codeine, opioids were more effective than nonopioids (SMD 0.30, 95% CI 0.15-­ 0.45). However, there were more adverse events associated with opioids (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.04-­ 3.42). Conclusions: For ED-­ discharged patients with acute musculoskeletal pain, opioids do not seem to be more effective than nonopioid analgesics. However, this absence of efficacy seems to be driven by codeine, as opioids other than codeine are more effective than nonopioids (mostly NSAIDs). Further prospective studies on the efficacy of short-­ term opioid use after ED discharge (excluding codeine), measuring patient-­ centered outcomes, adverse events, and potential misuse, are needed.

top_evidence.text: Risk of bias was assessed using the Effective Practice and Organization of Care (EPOC) risk-­ of-­ bias tool. 31 Two reviewers (JP and MM) assessed the risk of bias independently, with conflicts resolved through discussion or involvement of a third reviewer (RD). RCTs were ranked as having low risk, being unclear, or having high risk of bias across nine domains (i.e., random sequence generation, allocation concealment, similarity of baseline outcome measurements, similarity of baseline characteristics, incomplete outcome data, knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately prevented during the study, protection against contamination, selective outcome reporting, and other risk of bias) and the overall risk of bias was derived. Risk-­ of-­ bias judgments for each domain across studies were summarized using risk-­ of-­ bias graphs and summaries. Unpublished studies were considered at high risk of bias.

elements.quote: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Additionally, opioids were associated in all studies with a higher rate of adverse events and in one study with higher use of rescue medications.

elements.quote: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.
elements.reason: The Limitations section explicitly describes multiple limitations of the included evidence (heterogeneity of populations, interventions and follow-up, limited external validity, concomitant medications, and lack of assessment of long-term harms), fulfilling the requirement to discuss limitations of the evidence.

elements.quote: Sensitivity analyses were performed for studies with available short-­ term follow-­ up (≤3 days) to examine whether opioids were more effective in this situation. Another sensitivity analysis compared patients treated with codeine versus those treated with other opioids since codeine is a prodrug and its analgesic properties depend on its conversion to morphine, which varies considerably between subjects. 33 Sensitivity analyses were also performed excluding studies with high risk of bias and for studies involving a pediatric population compared to adults. Finally, we repeated the same analyses while excluding studies for which the comparator was only a placebo.

elements.quote: Our review is limited by the study population's heterogeneity (pediatric and adult), medications type/dosage, and follow-­ up duration. However, analyses were done using a random-­ effect | model, which partially compensated for this diversity and after excluding codeine, the heterogeneity was very low ( I 2 = 0%). Furthermore, results were consistent in sensitivity analyses on the adult population and in which the study with high risk of bias and the one with only placebo as a comparison was excluded. Also, we studied only opioid use after ED discharge; results could be different in another context. Most studies utilized extensive exclusion criteria and included only patients with musculoskeletal injuries in a North American population, which limit their external validity. The adult studies included only painful syndromes of sprains and strains, and none had fractures that might have been better relieved by opioids. Most included studies (five of six) used a combination of acetaminophen (one also added an NSAID) and opioid (two of them at higher acetaminophen doses than what is currently permitted) instead of opioid alone, which may have contributed to opioid efficacy. Finally, included studies were not designed to assess the risk of overdose, opioid use disorder, or long-­ term harms.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly states multiple limitations of the included evidence (population heterogeneity, medications/dosage, follow-up duration, ED discharge context, external validity constraints, restricted injury types, concomitant acetaminophen/NSAID regimens, and lack of assessment of overdose/OUD/long-term harms).
